tip: 'Trouver' here means 'find' in the sense of opinion: 'tu la trouves comment ?' = what do you think of her/it, literally 'how do you find her?'
'Y' replaces 'à + thing': 'croire à' (believe in) collapses to 'y croire' – 'tu y crois' = do you believe in it.
'Depuis' + the present tense = have been doing: 'nous y pensons depuis longtemps' = we've been thinking about it for a long time. French stays in the present.
For body parts French uses 'the' plus an indirect pronoun, not a possessive: 'lui a coupé les cheveux' = cut his hair, literally 'cut him the hair'.
'Veuillez' is the formal command form of 'vouloir' (to want), used for polite requests.
'Apprendre' stacks two 'à's: 'à' a person, 'à' an action. 'Il leur a appris à nager' = he taught them to swim ('leur' = to them, 'à nager' = to swim).
'En' stands in for 'any/some' of a thing: 'tu ne m'en as pas donné' = you didn't give me any. English can drop 'any', but French keeps 'en'.
'Demander à quelqu'un' = ask someone. French asks TO a person, so the pronoun is 'lui', not 'le': 'nous lui avons demandé son avis'.
'Son'/'sa' agree with the thing owned, not the owner: 'son sac' = her (or his) bag, because 'sac' is masculine. The owner's gender is invisible.
'Savoir' in the future often means 'find out', not just 'know': 'je saurai la réponse demain' = I'll learn the answer tomorrow.
'Parler de' something = talk about it, and 'de' + thing collapses to 'en': 'ils en parlent' = they talk about it. 'En' sits before the verb.
'Me' + 'en': the indirect pronoun comes before 'en'; 'me' drops its e before a vowel, giving 'm'en'.
French says 'less loud' for 'more quietly': 'parle moins fort' = speak more softly. 'Fort' is the go-to word for volume, not 'loudly'.
'Attendre' already means 'wait FOR' – no preposition follows: 'tu les attends' = you're waiting for them. Never add 'pour'.
'Jusqu'à ce que' (until) triggers the subjunctive: 'jusqu'à ce que le bus arrive'.
'Retrouver' = meet up with someone by arrangement (literally re-find them), not meet for the first time: 'tu le retrouves après le travail ?'
Weather uses 'faire' (to make), not 'être': 'il fait chaud' = it's hot, literally 'it makes hot'. Same for 'il fait froid', 'il fait beau'.
After 'quand', French uses the future where English uses the present: 'quand vous aurez fini' = when you're done, literally 'will have finished'. Both actions stay future.
'En' + the -ant form = 'while/on doing': 'en rentrant' = on your way home, while heading back. French compresses 'while returning' into 'en' + verb.
To say why you're going somewhere, French can just add a bare infinitive – no 'pour' needed: 'j'irai au marché acheter des fruits' = go to the market to buy fruit.
'Dès' + a noun = 'as soon as': 'dès notre arrivée' = the moment we arrive. Where English needs a whole clause, French uses 'dès' + noun.
Expressions of emotion ('triste', 'content', 'surpris') + 'que' trigger the subjunctive: 'triste que vous partiez'.
'Le' replaces a masculine singular noun, 'him' or 'it', and goes before the verb: 'je le vois' = I see him.
French can't say 'want you to come' with an infinitive: 'vouloir que' forces the subjunctive – 'nous voulons que vous veniez'.
'Aller' + infinitive is the everyday spoken future, like English 'going to': 'on va essayer' = we're going to try. Far more common in speech than 'on essaiera'.
Negative 'penser' triggers the subjunctive: 'je ne pense pas que ce soit'. Positive 'penser' takes the plain form: 'je pense que c'est'.
The past participle agrees with 'la' when it comes before the verb: 'nous la lui avons offerte' – feminine 'la', so 'offerte'.
A past participle never agrees with an indirect object: 'lui' sits before the verb, yet 'prêté' stays bare in 'je lui ai prêté ma voiture'.
'Il faut que' + subjunctive is the most common subjunctive trigger. 'Prennes' = subjunctive of 'prendre'.
'Quoi que' (whatever) triggers the subjunctive: 'quoi que tu dises' = whatever you say.
